title: Приёмка продуктов и сонные улитки  (Inspecting the Delivery and Sleepy Snails)

segments.t: Testing his new authority as sous-chef, Max orders the staff to put away the vegetables and meat before inspecting a crate of Burgundy snails brought by supplier Timur. Max suspects the motionless snails are dead, while Timur insists they are merely sleeping.
Так, овощи на склад, мясо в холодильник.
А что, думаешь, сами не догадаются?
Пойду займусь какой-нибудь фигней, может, приготовлю чем-нибудь.
Ага, давай.
Еще улитки.
Нет, просто спят.
Лучшие в городе.
Зачем нам столько пропавших улиток?
Ну ты сам посмотри.
Ну у нее вид.
Ну явно пропавшая.
Ты к чему рассказал, не самый свежий?
Ну ты даешь огузок.
Now let's break down each line of their conversation.
Так, овощи на склад, мясо в холодильник.
'Alright, vegetables to the storage room, meat into the fridge.' Max anchors the line on 'like this', while 'refrigerator' completes the thought. Chef Viktor answers right away.
А что, думаешь, сами не догадаются?
'What, do you think they cannot figure that out themselves?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'and' and finishing on 'to guess'.
Пойду займусь какой-нибудь фигней, может, приготовлю чем-нибудь.
'I will go busy myself with some nonsense, maybe cook something.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'go' before landing on 'with something'.
Ага, давай.
'Yeah, go right ahead.' The grammar packs 'yeah' and 'let's' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Chef Viktor answers right away.
Еще улитки.
'And here are the snails.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'else' and finishing on 'snail'.
Нет, просто спят.
'No, they are simply sleeping.' Lyova brings out the contrast between 'there is no' and 'just' in a few short words.
Лучшие в городе.
'The finest ones in the city.' The meaning hinges on 'best' working together with 'town' in spoken Russian. Chef Viktor answers right away.
Зачем нам столько пропавших улиток?
'Why do we need so many spoiled snails?' The grammar packs 'what for' and 'snail' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
Ну ты сам посмотри.
'Well, take a look for yourself.' Lyova brings out the contrast between 'come on' and 'you' in a few short words.
Ну у нее вид.
'Just look at the state of this one.' In Russian, the idea of 'come on' flows naturally into 'appearance' without extra filler words. Chef Viktor answers right away.
Ну явно пропавшая.
'It is obviously dead and spoiled.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'come on' before landing on 'missing'.
Ты к чему рассказал, не самый свежий?
'Why did you say they are not the freshest?' Lyova addresses the listener with the informal singular 'you' alongside 'fresh'.
Ну ты даешь огузок.
'Man, you really are something, Oguzok.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'come on' and finishing on 'Rump'. Now let's put it all back together and hear the whole scene again.
